papers.title: Nonclassicality of a Macroscopic Qubit-Ensemble via Parity Measurement Induced Disturbance
papers.summary: We propose an experimental scheme to test the nonclassicality of a macroscopic ensemble of qubits, through the violation of the classical notion of macrorealism (MR) via the fundamental measurement-induced disturbance of quantum systems. An electromagnetic resonator is used to probe the parity of the qubit-ensemble. The action of sequential measurements allows the nonclassicality of whole ensemble to manifest itself, in the ideal case, irrespective of its size. This enables to probe the macroscopic limits of quantum mechanics as the qubit-ensemble is, effectively, a single large spin of many $\hbar$ units. Even as $\hbar \rightarrow 0$ in comparison to the total angular momentum of the ensemble, a constant amount of violation of MR is found in the noiseless case. However, environmental decoherence and inhomogeneity of qubit-electromagnetic field couplings precipitate the quantum-to-classical transition. This illustrates that Bohr's correspondence principle is not fundamental, but a consequence of practical limitations. We outline an implementation with a variety of qubits (superconducting qubits, spins in semiconductors, and Rydberg atoms) coupled to a coplanar waveguide resonator, and -- via the corresponding noise analysis -- find that violation of MR is detectable up to $100$ qubits via current technology.

papers.title: Quantum measurement retrodiction and entropic uncertainty relations
papers.summary: We study quantum measurement retrodiction using the principle of minimum change. For quantum-to-classical measurement channels, we show that all standard quantum divergences select the same retrodictive update, yielding a unique and divergence-independent quantum Bayesian inverse for any POVM and prior state. Using this update, we construct a symmetric joint distribution for pairs of POVMs and introduce the mutual retrodictability, for which we also derive a general upper bound that depends only on the prior state and holds for all measurements. This structure leads to two retrodictive entropic uncertainty relations, expressed directly in terms of the prior state and the POVMs, but valid independently of the retrodictive framework and fully compatible with the conventional operational interpretation of entropic uncertainty relations. Finally, we benchmark these relations numerically and find that they provide consistently tighter bounds than existing entropic uncertainty relations over broad classes of measurements and states.

papers.title: Quantum Sensing using Geometrical Phase in Qubit-Oscillator Systems
papers.summary: We present a quantum sensing protocol for coupled qubit-oscillator systems that surpasses the standard quantum limit (SQL) by exploiting a geometrical phase. The signal is encoded in the geometrical phase that is proportional to the area enclosed in oscillator phase space. This area is amplified through squeezing, enabling sensitivities beyond the SQL. Our method is independent of oscillator's initial state, amenable to sensing with high-temperature or logical error-corrected states. The protocol shows robustness to qubit Markovian noise and preserves its state-independence, underscoring its practicality for next-generation quantum metrology. We demonstrate application to force sensing beyond the SQL in longitudinally coupled systems, and to high-precision measurements of couplings and pulse calibration surpassing SQL in dispersively coupled circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architectures.

papers.title: Frequency-matching quantum key distribution
papers.summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure communication against eavesdropping. However, phase instability remains a challenge across many QKD applications, particularly in schemes such as twin-field QKD and measurement-device-independent QKD. The most dominant source of phase fluctuation arises from the frequency offset between independent lasers. Here we propose a method to address this issue by employing a classical photodiode to compensate for the laser frequency difference. As an application of this method, we implement this technique in a mode-pairing QKD system, achieving an error rate approaching the theoretical limit and surpassing the linear key-rate bound over a fiber distance of 296.8 km. This approach provides a practical solution for frequency matching between independent lasers and can be extended to other fields requiring precise phase stabilization.

papers.title: On the relevance of Hermitian-preserving trace-preserving linear maps in asymptotic information retrieval in quantum communication
papers.summary: In quantum technologies, quantum channels are essential for transmitting quantum states. Quantum channels usually introduce noise, thereby reducing the information in a state. These are mathematically described by completely positive trace-preserving linear maps that represent the generic evolution of quantum systems and are also special cases of Hermitian-preserving trace-preserving (HPTP) linear maps. Concatenating a quantum channel with another quantum channel makes it noisier and degrades its information and resource preservability. In this work, we demonstrate a physically meaningful way to compare a pair of quantum channels using Hermitian-preserving trace-preserving linear maps. Precisely, given a pair of quantum channels $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2$ and an arbitrary unknown input state, we show that the output state of the quantum channel $\Lambda_2$ from the pair can be uniquely identified from the output statistics of the other channel $\Lambda_1$ from the pair, using some POVM, iff $\Lambda_2$ can be obtained from $\Lambda_1$ by concatenating it with a Hermitian-preserving trace-preserving linear map that is not necessarily positive. In such cases, $\Lambda_2$ may not always be obtained from $\Lambda_1$ through post-processing. The relation between these channels is a preorder, and we study its characterization in this work. In other words, we provide an operational interpretation of this preorder induced by HPTP linear maps in a communication scenario. Furthermore, we characterize the difficulty of implementing $\Lambda_2$ given that $\Lambda_1$ has already been implemented via a quantifier, namely, physical implementability. We also illustrate the implications of our results for the incompatibility of quantum devices through an example. In short, we provide valuable insights about the relevance of Hermitian-preserving trace-preserving linear maps in physically motivated settings.

papers.title: Deep Thermalization and Measurements of Quantum Resources
papers.summary: Quantum resource theories provide a unified framework for characterizing useful quantum phenomena subject to physical constraints, but are notoriously hard to assess in experimental systems. In this letter, we introduce a unified protocol for quantifying the resource-generating power of arbitrary quantum evolutions applicable to multiple resource theories. It is based on deep thermalization, which has recently gained attention for its role in the emergence of quantum state designs from partial projective measurements. Central to our approach is the use of projected ensembles, recently employed to probe deep thermalization, together with new twirling identities that allow us to directly infer the resource-generating powers of the underlying dynamics. These identities further reveal how resources build up and thermalize in generic quantum circuits. Finally, we show that quantum resources themselves undergo deep thermalization at the subsystem level, offering a complementary and another experimentally accessible route to infer the resource-generating powers. Our work connects deep thermalization to resource quantification, offering a new perspective on the essential role of various resources in generating state designs and on efficient estimation of quantum resources in experiment.

papers.title: Certified bounds on optimization problems in quantum theory
papers.summary: Semidefinite relaxations of polynomial optimization have become a central tool for addressing the non-convex optimization problems over non-commutative operators that are ubiquitous in quantum information theory and, more in general, quantum physics. Yet, as these global relaxation methods are solved numerically, the bounds issued by the semidefinite solver can - and often do - exceed the global optimum, undermining their certifiability. To counter this issue, we introduce a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds on non-commutative optimization problems from inexact numerical data, and apply it to several paradigmatic problems in quantum information theory. An extension to sparsity and symmetry-adapted semidefinite relaxations is also provided and compared to the general dense scheme. Our results establish rational post-processing as a practical route to reliable certification, pushing semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science.

papers.title: Geometric Complexity of Quantum Channels via Unitary Dilations
papers.summary: Nielsen's geometric approach to quantum circuit complexity provides a Riemannian framework for quantifying the cost of implementing unitary closed-system dynamics. For open evolutions, the reduced dynamics is described by time-dependent families of quantum channels $\{\Lambda_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ admitting many inequivalent Stinespring realizations, so any meaningful complexity notion must specify which microscopic resources are counted and which transformations are treated as gauge. We develop a dilation-based geometric complexity framework that distinguishes implementation-dependent complexity, attached to a specific realization, from intrinsic channel complexity obtained by minimizing over a physically admissible class of dilations. The proposed functional is subtractive: it removes purely environmental contributions from the geometric cost of the joint unitary realization. The subtraction is derived from concise structural postulates --- closed-system consistency, environment-only neutrality, and invariance under dilation gauge transformations --- and admits a natural variational and geometric interpretation. We also define noise complexity as a companion quantity measuring the geometric deviation of a noisy implementation from a prescribed ideal closed-system evolution. In the Hilbert-Schmidt setting, we establish coherence-based lower bounds for unitary and noise complexity, prove linear time scaling under time-homogeneous dilation models, and obtain dissipator-controlled bounds in the Markovian GKSL regime. We illustrate the framework on canonical single-qubit benchmark channels: dephasing, amplitude damping, and Pauli/depolarizing noise.

papers.title: Classical Analog Emulation of Quantum Circuits via Time-Averaged Dynamic States
papers.summary: Between the digital and quantum paradigms lies the emerging field of quantum-inspired analog computing, in which classical waves emulate quantum circuits. We introduce wavebits -- classical wave analogs of qubits whose amplitudes are carried by physical oscillatory signals -- and show that any nonseparable N-qubit state can be encoded in 2N narrowband signals that remain locally separable at every instant; the nonseparable correlations are recovered at readout by time-averaged demodulation over auxiliary carrier frequencies, the nonseparability channels. We prove that any two-qubit gate unravels into the time-averaged tensor product of two local time-varying operators, and that arbitrary circuits are emulated with a base-frequency count scaling linearly in the number of entangling two-qubit gates, independent of qubit number for a fixed gate count. The exponential cost of the 2^N-dimensional state reappears at readout and in the averaging time of circuits with many two-qubit gates, not in circuit execution, as quantified by an analytic error bound that doubles as a hardware design rule. A mixed-signal prototype emulates Bell state generation, controlled-NOT gates, phase kickback, and Bloch-sphere rotations at fidelities above 0.99, and numerical benchmarks against exact statevectors validate the scheme for up to six qubits. The architecture is directly implementable in acoustic, photonic, and mixed-signal platforms.

papers.summary: This work provides a step-by-step quantum computing derivation of the unitary coupled cluster singles and doubles ansatz. We exemplify the procedure on the singles and doubles coupled cluster ansatz for the hydrogen molecule.

papers.title: On the Redfield and Lindblad master equations
papers.summary: In a previous work we developed a field theoretical approach to open quantum systems using condensed matter methods. In the Born approximation we derived the Redfield equation on the basis of a multi-oscillator bath, a Dyson equation, a diagrammatic expansion and a quasi-particle approximation. In addition applying a rotating wave approximation we obtained the Lindblad equation describing a proper quantum map. The issue regarding the additional rotating wave approximation was left as an open problem. The present work addresses the open problem and presents new results. We identify a discrepancy in the popular and standard Redfield equation. The discrepancy is associated with the well-known fact that the Redfield equation does not represent a proper quantum map. The discrepancy is related to the diagrammatic expansion and a consistency requirement in the quasi-particle approximation. The explicit resolution of this discrepancy is obtained by imposing energy conservation on the Born level. As a result we obtain formal equivalence between the energy-conserving Redfield equation and the Lindblad equation without invoking the rotating wave approximation. We provide a detailed mapping of the field theoretical approach to the standard microscopic derivation in the theory of open quantum systems.

papers.title: Tensor Decomposition for Non-Clifford Gate Minimization
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires substantial resources for non-Clifford gates. Their count also enters exponentially into the runtime of several classical simulation methods. We present algebraic methods for minimizing the non-Clifford CCZ (Toffoli) count in {CNOT,CCZ} phase circuits using tensor decomposition over $\mathbb{F}_2$. On standard cubic benchmarks, these methods match or improve prior automated Toffoli counts, with most instances optimized in under a minute on a single CPU. With additional computation, the decompositions provide effective initializations for existing T-count methods, improving T counts on several circuits. We also present algebraic methods for CNOT-count optimization at fixed Toffoli count. This gives competitive ancilla-free finite-field multiplication circuits and reduces the CNOT count of XOR AES S-box circuits.

papers.title: QwaveMPS: An efficient open-source Python package for simulating non-Markovian waveguide-QED using matrix product states
papers.summary: QwaveMPS is an open-source Python library for simulating one-dimensional quantum many-body waveguide systems using matrix product states (MPS). It provides a user-friendly interface for constructing, evolving, and analyzing quantum states and operators, facilitating studies in quantum physics and quantum information with waveguide-QED systems. This approach enables efficient, scalable simulations by focusing computational resources on the most relevant parts of the quantum system. Thus, one can study a wide range of complex dynamical interactions, including time-delayed feedback effects in the non-Markovian regime and deeply nonlinear systems, at a highly reduced computational cost compared to full Hilbert space approaches, making it both practical and convenient to model a variety of open waveguide-QED systems (in Markovian and non-Markovian regimes), treating quantized atoms and quantized photons on an equal footing. The QwaveMPS package automates the waveguide-QED-specific tensor-network operations, including construction of the time-bin evolution operator from physical parameters, the swap network required for delayed interactions, orthogonality-center and truncation management, the matrix-product factorization of $N$-photon Fock-state inputs, and the evaluation of single-time and two-time field observables (such as the second-order quantum correlation function) at chosen points along the waveguide.

papers.title: A rigorous hybridization of variational quantum eigensolver with classical neural network
papers.summary: Combining variational quantum process with classical neural learning offers a flexible route to improve ground-state estimation. We establish an integrated framework that connects neural transformations, measurement statistics, and physical stability through three requirements: self-contained training, polynomial resource scaling, and variational consistency. Its constructive realization, termed unitary variational quantum-neural hybrid eigensolver (U-VQNHE), couples a variational quantum circuit to a neural phase function through norm-preserving post-processing. The learned transformation is evaluated from measurement records, preserves the exact variational bound, and admits range-independent concentration guarantees for independent finite-shot evaluations. Complementing this construction, we characterize the statistical and representational constraints of amplitude reweighting: sampled-support mismatch can destabilize empirical normalization, while polynomial-range reweighting exactly matches only an exponentially small fraction of Haar-random target distributions from a fixed ansatz, and exact matching for structured ansatz--target pairs can require exponentially large dynamic range under specified near-tensorizability and mismatch conditions. Finite-shot simulations on Ising and disordered XYZ spin models demonstrate improved energy accuracy over the underlying variational quantum eigensolver and greater robustness than the amplitude-reweighting baselines. Together, these results provide a principled foundation for quantum--neural eigensolvers in which physical consistency, expressive capacity, and measurement cost are treated as a single design problem.

papers.title: Theory and interpretability of Quantum Extreme Learning Machines: a Pauli transfer matrix approach
papers.summary: Quantum reservoir computers (QRCs) have emerged as a promising approach to quantum machine learning, since they utilize the natural dynamics of quantum systems for data processing and are simple to train. Here, we consider $n$-qubit quantum extreme learning machines (QELMs) with initial-state encoding and continuous-time reservoir dynamics. Applying the Pauli transfer matrix (PTM) formalism reveals the encoding-generated features and their linear transformation by quantum channels, and thereby provides a nonlinear vector autoregression model as an interpretable classical representation of a QELM. We show that the nonlinear information processing capacity of a QELM factorizes into the ability of the encoding to represent a given target function and the decodability of the relevant Pauli features after the effective PTM. Comparing geometric and statistical decodability reveals features that are algebraically hidden yet recoverable through data correlations. We relate the decodability of Pauli features to the spreading of measurement operators under Heisenberg evolution (Krylov growth). Focusing on the unitary channel, we discuss how structured Hamiltonians, when paired with certain observables, can impair model performance, as reflected in a low rank of the readout and the effective PTMs. We trace this effect to Hamiltonian symmetries and derive asymptotic rank estimates for symmetry-resolved observable families. Our decodability analysis disentangles the contributions of encoding, reservoir dynamics, and measurement observables, and thus provides interpretable diagnostics that can inform the design of QELMs and reduce reliance on exhaustive hyperparameter search. As a specific application, we consider forecasting nonlinear dynamical systems and show that the readout of a trained QELM closely matches the expression of the underlying flow map at leading orders.

papers.title: Control of Multipartite Entanglement through Anisotropy against Thermal Noise

Using a master-equation approach combined with the Bethe ansatz technique, we show analytically that robustness of multipartite entanglement at low temperatures can be enhanced by suitably tuning the anisotropy of the system. Our results highlight interaction-induced spectral control as a mechanism for stabilizing multipartite entanglement in quantum computing platforms.

papers.title: A Scalable, Optimized Scheduler for the Active Volume Architecture
papers.summary: We improve the accuracy of Active Volume (AV) resource estimates by explicitly scheduling when AV blocks execute and when their reactions complete. We present a cycle-accurate scheduler that assigns each logical qubit a role in every logical cycle. The approach allows us to capture execution effects such as gate packing inefficiencies, parallelization overhead, and memory requirements. In addition, the scheduler explicitly tracks reaction latency and stale state lifetimes, rather than assuming that stale states can be absorbed into a fixed overhead. For a $4\times4$ Fermi--Hubbard test circuit, we find a transition to reaction-dominant regime at approximately $10^3$ logical qubits. Beyond $10^3$ logical qubits, stale state accumulation restricts the effective workspace and the benefit of adding more qubits is substantially decreased. Below this regime the scheduler predicts a $1.64\times$ runtime speedup relative to the previous Analytic Resource Estimators (ARE), primarily due to a $1.80\times$ reduction in average memory occupancy. We also show that parallelization and reaction latency overhead grows with available workspace, inverting the trend of the ARE model used in \cite{Caesura25}. These results provide a path toward reaction-aware analytic resource estimates and a full compilation pipeline for AV architectures. We also develop novel techniques for estimating Y state and routing demand and apply them to our test circuit. The Y state estimates result in small efficiency boost and the routing demand estimates show that routing should not bottleneck early fault-tolerant AV devices.

papers.title: Quantifying entanglement in quantum thermodynamics via separability constraints
papers.summary: The role of quantum entanglement in thermodynamical systems remains elusive. Does entanglement result in thermodynamic advantages or does it impose fundamental limitations? Here, we unambiguously quantify the amount of heat and work in a quantum system that is due to the presence of entanglement. This is achieved by constraining the system's non-equilibrium dynamics to separable states, thereby isolating the impact entanglement has on thermodynamic effects. Unlike thermodynamic entanglement measures, which signify a loose connection between entanglement and thermodynamic properties, imposing a constraint constitutes an active intervention into a system -- answering how much of a system's thermodynamics is caused by (not correlated with) its quantumness. We benchmark our theory by applying the constrained dynamics to several multipartite systems, including quantum batteries and quantum refrigerators.

papers.title: Bounding the entanglement of a state from its spectrum
papers.summary: We introduce a framework to upper bound the entanglement content of a bipartite quantum state from its spectrum alone. We use as entanglement quantifiers the negativity and the Schmidt number; however, our framework is general and applies to any other entanglement measure. Our approach yields compact analytical sufficient criteria for bounding the entanglement of full-rank states in arbitrary dimensions and reveals new spectral constraints on Schmidt number witnesses.

papers.title: Qurator: Scheduling Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows Across Heterogeneous Cloud Providers
papers.summary: We present Qurator, a quantum-classical task scheduler that jointly optimizes queue time and circuit fidelity across heterogeneous architectures. Qurator models hybrid workloads as dynamic DAGs with explicit quantum semantics, including entanglement dependencies, synchronization barriers, no-cloning constraints, and circuit cutting and merging decisions. Fidelity is estimated through a unified logarithmic success score that reconciles incompatible calibration data from IBM, IonQ, IQM, Rigetti, AQT, Pasqal and other providers into a canonical set of gate error, readout fidelity, and decoherence terms. We evaluate Qurator on a simulator driven by four months of real queue data using circuits from the Munich Quantum Toolkit benchmark suite. Across load conditions from 5 to 35,000 quantum tasks with up to 120,000 classical tasks, Qurator stays within 1% of the highest-fidelity baseline at low load, achieves 30-75% queue time reduction at high load, all at a fidelity cost bounded by a user-specified target while improving on list and fair schedulers as well as state of the art schedulers on both metrics.

papers.title: Low Depth Distributed Quantum Algorithms for Unordered Database Search
papers.summary: Grover's algorithm accelerates unstructured database search quadratically compared to classical algorithms. In the NISQ era, distributed quantum computing can decrease circuit depth and reduce noise. In this paper, an algorithm for constructing query operators for subfunctions is proposed. By dividing the target string of the search problem into several substrings and integrating the query operator of each subfunction, a low-depth distributed exact quantum search algorithm is designed. The contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) The proposed distributed algorithm has a lower circuit depth and can mitigate error accumulation compared to distributed quantum search algorithms; (2) The target can be accurately located by the proposed distributed algorithm; (3) Experiments conducted with the quantum software MindQuantum confirm the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed distributed algorithm. Moreover, the introduction of noise to the circuit during these experiments indicates that the algorithm possesses an inherent capacity for noise resistance.

papers.title: Robustness Evaluation of Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks under Noise Models via System-Level Error Mitigation
papers.summary: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) represent a promising direction within Quantum Machine Learning (QML), yet their realization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remains constrained by decoherence, gate imperfections, crosstalk, and readout errors. This study provides a systematic evaluation of noise effects and mitigation strategies in hybrid quantum neural networks (HQNNs). Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), Digital Dynamical Decoupling (DDD), and Layerwise Richardson Extrapolation (LRE) are incorporated into end-to-end QNN training pipelines developed with PennyLane, simulated using Qiskit Aer noise models, and integrated with the Mitiq framework, while Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) is evaluated separately under depolarizing noise due to its computational cost. Experiments conducted on the Iris dataset with five representative noise channels show that the impact of noise and the effect of mitigation are strongly dependent on the noise model and its strength. The model maintains comparatively strong performance under phase-flip and phase-damping noise, while substantial degradation is observed under high depolarizing and amplitude-damping noise. Across the evaluated mitigation methods, the observed benefits remain limited and noise-dependent: ZNE, DDD, and LRE generally follow the same degradation trends as the unmitigated baseline, while PEC shows limited gains only in the low-noise depolarizing regime. These findings highlight the need for context-specific mitigation strategies to improve the robustness of QNNs in practical NISQ settings.

papers.title: Randomized Subsystem Descent for Fermion-to-Qubit Mapping
papers.summary: We propose a versatile and efficient algorithmic framework for optimizing fermion-to-qubit mappings by generalizing the idea of randomized block coordinate descent. Our greedy approach, termed Randomized Subsystem Descent, iteratively samples a tractable subsystem from the full Hamiltonian, performs optimization within the subsystem under a given metric, and then reintegrates the updated subsystem into the global operator. Restricting the optimization to a subsystem at each iteration ensures computational efficiency, bypassing the dimensional bottlenecks that usually hinder global search heuristics. We benchmark our algorithm on one- and two-dimensional lattice hopping models, the Hubbard model with up to $16 \times 16$ sites, alongside a collection of molecular electronic-structure Hamiltonians with up to $54$ modes and more than $180,000$ Pauli strings. Across all benchmarks, our method consistently provides appreciable reduction in (weighted) Pauli weight, suggesting that Randomized Subsystem Descent is a practical and scalable framework for lowering the resource overhead of finding hardware-efficient Hamiltonian encodings.

papers.title: Entanglement and reciprocal dynamics of the Barnett and Einstein-de Haas responses in a quantum spin-rotor model
papers.summary: We study the reciprocal Barnett and Einstein--de Haas effects in an exactly solvable quantum spin--rotor model that conserves the total angular momentum. For a single spin-$1/2$, the model describes rotation-dependent spin polarization, coherent transfer of angular momentum between the spin and the rotor, and the accompanying spin--rotor entanglement. At a recoil-compensation point, all angular-momentum sectors become synchronized, allowing complete spin reversal and a one-quantum shift of an arbitrary rotor wave packet. We then extend the model to two spins coupled to the same rotor, where the shared rotational degree of freedom participates dynamically in the generation of spin--spin entanglement. The singlet forms a dark state, while the triplet sector remains coupled to the mechanical motion. At a special parameter point, the rotor returns to its original dynamical branch and disentangles from the spins, leaving behind a maximally entangled two-spin state locally equivalent to a Bell state.

papers.title: Exploiting all ancilla outcomes in linear combinations of unitaries: low-rank recovery and quantum trapdoor functions
papers.summary: The linear combination of unitaries (LCU) is a fundamental quantum computing primitive used to embed non-unitary operators into larger systems via ancilla post-selection. In standard LCU implementations, only the zero-state ancilla outcome is retained, while all other measurement branches are discarded as unusable overhead. We study these discarded parts. Every computational-basis outcome of the ancilla projects the system onto a different linear combination of the target unitaries; collecting these outcome states in a matrix gives a factorization $\Phi=CX$, where $C$ is determined by the ancilla preparation and the rows of $X$ are the states $U_t|\psi\rangle$, so that $rank(\Phi)\le K$. Although this holds for any LCU circuit; to make the analysis easier, we use a simplified model circuit with Hadamard gates on the index register and a single rotation qubit in place of the coefficient preparation unitary, in which $C$ is explicit. The structure suggests two complementary applications: (i) in an explicit amplitude-access model, classical low-rank matrix completion can reconstruct the full output (including the target) from a subset of its amplitude entries, while computational basis counts provide intensities and generally require additional phase information for full complex recovery; (ii) treating $C$ as a secret key suggests a candidate quantum trapdoor function, whose security remains informal and depends on the difficulty of structured phase retrieval. The scheme thus turns the "junk" ancilla outcomes into a structured resource, possibly opening paths for further applications.

papers.title: Neural Information Causality: A Random-Access Capacity Law for Representation Learning
papers.summary: How can a learned representation remain useful when the question it must answer is chosen only after encoding? Preserving information is essential, but does not by itself ensure access to the requested target. We address this problem by deriving "neural information causality (Neural-IC)," a representation law that connects causal access to the physically specified interface capacity. For a fresh database of independent bits, the aggregate information recoverable across later queries cannot exceed that capacity, even with pre-established quantum resources. A decomposition separates capacity slack, information organized jointly across targets, and losses in producing answers. Exhaustive evaluation of trained binary codes reveals why nearly full use of a memory's information budget can coexist with limited retrieval. In a nested Bell-correlation construction, quantum assistance improves average retrieval over the optimal classical one-bit benchmark within the same communicated budget. These results give representation learning a design principle that connects information capacity to the organization and extraction of target information. By locating the constraints on later answers, the framework can inform memory allocation, encoding objectives, and decoder outputs, providing a basis for seeking better retrieval within a fixed budget.

papers.title: Freezing-Induced Interaction Engineering in Fixed-Frequency Transmon Networks
papers.summary: Freezing is usually used to suppress unwanted dynamics, but it can also be used to engineer interactions. We introduce freezing-induced interaction engineering, a drive-only control scheme in which a continuously driven auxiliary subsystem remains frozen while its drive-dependent state reshapes the effective Hamiltonian of neighboring degrees of freedom. We apply this idea to fixed-frequency transmon systems using a driven modulator coupled to a pivot transmon with fixed native exchange interactions to neighboring transmons. Changing only the modulator drive frequency controls the dressed resonance condition of the pivot, selectively activating a native interaction or detuning it from all neighbors. Full lab-frame simulations of multilevel transmons demonstrate this switching mechanism and show that it remains effective under finite-time frequency ramps. We further demonstrate the same control mechanism numerically in a four-transmon, two-neighbor setting, where changing only the modulator drive frequency selectively activates either neighboring native interaction or suppresses both. Repeating this local control unit along a fixed-frequency chain gives a scalable architecture for alternating layers of native iSWAP interactions.

papers.title: Towards Fair Benchmarking of Quantum Transfer Learning for Visual Classification
papers.summary: Quantum Transfer Learning (QTL) offers a promising approach for visual quantum machine learning under near-term constraints, where limited qubit counts, shallow circuit depths, and costly hybrid optimization restrict end-to-end quantum training. In this setting, pretrained classical backbones can extract high-level visual features, while compact quantum modules operate as trainable classification heads. However, existing QTL results are difficult to compare because they often differ in datasets, preprocessing, backbone settings, qubit budgets, circuit designs, optimization choices, and reporting protocols. This work presents a controlled benchmarking methodology for evaluating representative QTL methods under a unified transfer-learning pipeline. The benchmark compares DQN-QTL, QPIE-QTL, AE-CQTL, PVCQTL, and ED-QTL under shared preprocessing rules, frozen-backbone settings, training conditions, and reporting metrics. The evaluation focuses on Fashion-MNIST and Hymenoptera Ants vs. Bees as the two main datasets, while CIFAR-10 is used to provide additional configuration-level evidence on a harder natural-image task. Beyond predictive performance, the benchmark analyzes circuit size, trainable parameters, quantum parameters, training time, and architectural sensitivity to qubit count and circuit depth. The results show that no single QTL family dominates across all settings: performance depends on the dataset, encoding strategy, circuit design, and computational cost. These findings highlight the need for resource-aware QTL evaluation and provide guidance for selecting hybrid quantum-classical transfer models under near-term resource constraints.

papers.title: Impurity-induced loss bursts from anomalous scale-free localization in a non-Hermitian dissipative lattice
papers.summary: We identify anomalous scale-free localization and associated impurity-induced loss bursts in a non-Hermitian dissipative cross-stitch lattice. By a local basis rotation, the model is mapped onto an effective non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice, where local impurities act as tunable effective boundaries. For the parameter choice considered here, the impurity-free periodic-boundary-condition point is reached at $\eta=1$. Tuning $\eta$ away from this point drives the system through generalized-boundary-condition regimes toward two effective open-boundary-condition-like limits at $\eta\to0$ and $\eta\to\infty$. For finite $\eta\notin\{0,1\}$, the loop-sector spectra remain separated from the real-energy axis, while the corresponding eigenstates exhibit scale-free localization pinned by the impurity. Unlike conventional impurity-induced scale-free localization, the Lyapunov exponent depends explicitly on the eigenenergy, making the localization strength eigenstate dependent. We further show that this anomalous eigenmode structure produces an impurity-induced loss burst: The long-time integrated dissipation probability develops a pronounced local enhancement relative to the surrounding background near an impurity-generated effective boundary, even when the initial wave packet is prepared far away. In the single-impurity case, the burst region consists of the impurity site and its adjacent effective-boundary site, and the effect occurs without imaginary-gap closing. For multiple impurities, local burst regions emerge around all impurities, while the dominant burst boundary is selected by the initial wave-packet position and the nonreciprocal drift direction. These results connect anomalous scale-free localization with controllable dissipation dynamics in non-Hermitian lattices.

papers.title: Fate of Quantum Scars and Chaos-Assisted Tunneling under Dissipation
papers.summary: Quantum scars enable memory and recurrent dynamics, but their fate under dissipation remains poorly understood. Here, we show that distinct quantum scars can respond qualitatively differently to the same dissipative channel. We consider a collective spin model coupled to a lossy cavity and, guided by its classical limit, identify scars associated with two unstable structures: a saddle point on a dissipation-free invariant manifold with vanishing cavity field and an unstable superradiant fixed point with finite photon occupation. The former is immune to photon loss in the classical limit and exhibits persistent quantum revivals, whereas the latter couples directly to the dissipative channel, but exhibits slow dynamics. Remarkably, the superradiant scar also supports chaos-assisted quantum tunneling between two symmetry-related, macroscopically distinct semiclassical configurations, despite the presence of dissipation. Our results identify an experimentally accessible setting for exploring dissipative scarring and chaos-assisted tunneling in cavity QED.

papers.title: Homomorphic Quantum Error Correction
papers.summary: We study the algebraic compatibility between quantum homomorphic encryption and stabilizer quantum error correction in an honest-but-curious model, restricting the encryption to the transversal block-Pauli mask $(X^aZ^b)^{\otimes n}$ controlled by two secret key bits $a$ and $b$. We prove a necessary and sufficient criterion for an $[[n,1,d]]$ stabilizer code to remain compatible with this mask, namely that the transversal $X$ and $Z$ operators commute with every stabilizer generator, and we specialize it to a classical-code criterion for Calderbank--Shor--Steane codes. Combining code-space preservation with the logical action of the mask, every stabilizer code falls, with respect to each of the two transversal mask operators, into exactly one of three classes: incompatible, compatible but trivially acting, or compatible with a nontrivial logical Pauli action; the two operators need not fall into the same class. We verify this classification by exact symplectic computation for rotated and planar surface codes, toric codes, triangular and toric color codes, the $[[15,1,3]]$ code and several small codes, and find that the class is fixed by the lattice size and the boundary presentation rather than by the topological phase: the surface-code family realizes all three classes, whereas color codes realize only the two compatible ones. For encrypted computation we show that the Shor code does not implement the logical $T$ gate by a transversal $T^{\otimes 9}$, whereas suitable triorthogonal codes do so up to a Clifford correction. We formulate logical-Pauli masking as a code-independent algebraic template. Syndrome extraction and recovery are key-independent whenever the mask preserves the code space, so that the client only needs the block size and the class of the code to decrypt.

papers.title: PauLIB: HPC Strategies for Pauli-Arithmetic-Based Quantum Computing Workloads and Simulations
papers.summary: As quantum devices become accelerators within classical HPC deployments, the efficiency of the classical partition becomes critical. Workloads such as Hamiltonian manipulation, observable backpropagation, and Pauli-based compilation reduce to bulk arithmetic on Pauli strings and sums. We present HPC strategies for this arithmetic, demonstrated in PauLIB, a header-only C++20 library: a bit-packed binary symplectic representation reducing Pauli multiplication to a bitwise XOR and population count; a sorted, struct-of-arrays layout replacing hash maps and exposing contiguous word arrays to SIMD units and GPU warps; and deterministic OpenMP parallelism with race-free output partitioning. These strategies deliver orders-of-magnitude higher throughput and smaller memory footprint than Qiskit and PauliEngine, plus a speedup from a CUDA outer-product kernel on an H100. Two case studies, g-sim and truncated Pauli propagation, inherit these gains and scale unchanged from a desktop Arm CPU to a 72-core HPC Arm server. PauLIB is open source with C++ and Python interfaces.

papers.title: Quantum digital simulations of time-domain semiconductor spectroscopy in the semi-classical approximation
papers.summary: We present a digital quantum simulation framework for ultrafast optical spectroscopy of semiconductor materials. The framework is based on Brillouin-zone discretization and is designed as a quantum alternative to classical simulations based on the semiconductor Bloch equations. Its current capabilities include quantum simulations of linear absorption and optical gain, incorporating Lorentzian broadening, finite-temperature band-filling effects, and reduced-dimensionality effects. Comparison with classical simulations of GaAs within the single-particle approximation demonstrates quantitative agreement in the noiseless limit. The inclusion of realistic hardware noise characteristic of NISQ-era quantum computers effectively manifests as an additional source of scattering, resulting in increased spectral broadening. We also show that the linear optical response, including many-body interactions treated within the Hartree-Fock approximation, can be mapped onto a system of coupled classical oscillators. Under certain assumptions about the query complexity of the oscillator couplings, this system exhibits a provable quantum advantage, as demonstrated in [Phys. Rev. X 13, 041041 (2023)]. Beyond the Hartree-Fock approximation, classical simulations based on many-body quantum kinetic equations face the so-called hierarchy problem, whereas the algorithmic complexity of the quantum simulations remains unchanged, offering a promising approach to overcoming this challenge.

papers.title: QPredSGG: Hybrid Quantum Predicate Learning for Long-Tailed Scene Graph Generation
papers.summary: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) requires relational reasoning over objects and their interactions, but performance is constrained by long-tail predicate imbalance. Classical SGG models rely on dataset statistics, leading to biased predictions toward frequent relations rather than fine-grained semantic predicates. Although debiasing improves mean recall, predicate classification in existing frameworks still relies on high-dimensional classical decision modules with high parameter overhead. This work introduces a resource-efficient hybrid quantum predicate classifier for SGG by replacing the classical predicate head in the CFEN with a QP-Head trained using class-balanced WCE. To the best of our knowledge, this work is among the first evaluations of a hybrid quantum architecture for scene graph predicate classification on Visual Genome 150. We evaluate the impact of qubit count, encoding strategy, entangling topology, and circuit depth. Under a 4-qubit configuration using Amplitude Embedding and Strongly Entangling Layers, the QP-Head projects 4096-dimensional pair features into a 16-dimensional quantum input while using 96 trainable quantum parameters. Operating within this compressed representation space under WCE training, it achieves strong long-tail recognition, reaching a peak mR@100 of 57.25% compared to the 41.1% mR@100 reported in the CFEN baseline under standard training. Protocol-matched ablations indicate that the primary advantage of the quantum head lies in extreme representational compactness rather than an accuracy gain over full-dimensional weighted classical heads: it achieves global recall within 0.19pp of the 2048-dimensional WCE classical baseline while operating from a 128x smaller head feature space. Scaling to 8 qubits maintains robust long-tail performance (55.38% mR@100 with 384 quantum parameters), while depth analysis highlights expressibility-latency trade-offs.

papers.title: Dynamical Decoupling using Universal Optimal Tracking
papers.summary: Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a widely used and resource-efficient technique for error suppression, but conventional DD relies on periodically repeating a short pulse block to refocus the qubit state during idle periods. Imperfections in this block cause residual errors to accumulate, ultimately degrading state recovery over long idle times. Here, we introduce a universal optimal tracking approach that extends the original tracking concept to a fully state-independent setting for designing DD sequences. By monitoring the qubit's evolution at predefined waypoints during optimization, the method dynamically compensates residual errors while preserving regular refocusing. Experimental demonstrations on a superconducting-qubit platform confirm the suppression of error accumulation under static control imperfections, in agreement with numerical predictions. Complementary simulations further show that optimal-tracking-based sequences maintain strong performance under time-dependent noise. These results establish optimal tracking as a practical and hardware-agnostic approach to designing short, robust DD sequences suitable for noisy quantum devices.

papers.title: Quantum Imaging via Kurtosis-Difference Weighted Covariance on 2D Camera
papers.summary: Camera-based quantum imaging detects spatially correlated photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). Conventional covariance methods typically require tens of thousands of frames to extract weak correlations from noise. While thick crystals can increase photon flux, they generate photon pairs from multiple emission positions within the crystal, producing multiple correlation centers with complex pairing geometries. In addition, conventional covariance methods assume a single pre-selected correlation center and cannot fully exploit these distributed correlations. We demonstrate that kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic measuring tail similarity, effectively discriminates correlated pixel pairs even when correlation coefficients remain low. Weighting covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference can select symmetric pixels while preserving true coincidences. This kurtosis weighting automatically identifies correlated pairs within a broad search region and accommodates multiple pairing geometries without requiring precise correlation center calibration. At 5000 frames, our method yields a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) exceeding 7, whereas standard covariance remains below 2. Compared with standard covariance, the method reduces the acquisition time by 40-fold and could enable practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.

papers.title: Operational boundaries, threshold conditions, and self-quenching in single-emitter microcavity lasers
papers.summary: We theoretically examine the emission dynamics of a three-level cascade single-emitter microcavity laser using the open-system Lindblad master equation. In our numerical simulations, we expand the Hilbert space dimensions to obtain converged observables free from truncation artifacts. We notice that the intracavity field builds up continuously to a peak value of $\langle n_p \rangle_{\rm max}$, bypassing the sharp thermodynamic thresholds of conventional ensemble lasers. By tracking individual radiative rates and for the selected set of parameters, we isolate a physical threshold at a normalized pump rate of $\Gamma/\gamma_{12} \approx 2.45$, where net stimulated emission overcomes spontaneous noise. Crucially, comparing these numerical master equation solutions against factorized semiclassical models reveals that mean-field approximations omit a vital light-matter correlation drag force, leading to a substantial overestimation of the peak field intensity by more than 10\%. We notice that the transient Wigner function undergoes complete phase diffusion into a radially symmetric ring due to the absence of a phase-locking ensemble. Furthermore, steady-state noise calculations confirm that discrete incoherent pumping fluctuations restrict the field to strictly super-Poissonian statistics (with the Mandel parameter $Q > 0$ and the second-order coherence function with zero delay $g^{(2)}(0) > 1$), establishing the classical shot-noise limit as a strict lower bound. At high pumping rates, population trapping in the upper level creates an excitation bottleneck that suppresses the cavity field and causes self-quenching. Our results provide an essential baseline for optimizing solid-state quantum dot and color-center nanophotonic architectures for lasing as well as for the generation of non-classical states of light.

papers.title: Accuracy, Decision Risk, and Sampling Cost in Quantum Error Mitigation
papers.summary: Quantum error mitigation estimates expectation values that are often used to select or rank candidates. We study how estimation accuracy, decision risk and sampling cost are related in these tasks. The joint law of residual differences determines the risk of a shift-invariant decision; in Gaussian regimes, effective margins and their covariance provide a computable representation. This connects mitigation maps, shared measurement records and shot allocation, and yields an extrapolation design criterion under certified margins. Finite-shot QAOA-MaxCut controls illustrate two forms of this relationship: a positive affine CDR correction reduces mean-squared error while preserving rankings, whereas signed PEC sampling reduces mean-squared error and increases selection failures at equal evaluation cost. A retrospective, oracle-assisted study of 48 landscapes compares Gaussian-risk and MSE-based method selection using separate fitting, selection and evaluation samples. At the primary total shot budget, with learning amortized over 20 decisions per landscape, failure rates are $0.3083$ for Gaussian-risk selection, $0.4719$ for MSE selection and $0.2333$ for unmitigated estimation. These comparisons describe how uncertainty in candidate differences and the allocation of measurements between learning and evaluation jointly enter the assessment of mitigation.

papers.title: Decoherence of a quantum magneto-oscillator: Effect of field-bath interaction
papers.summary: We investigate the quantum dissipative dynamics of a charged magneto-oscillator(CMO) coupled to a heat bath of harmonic oscillators in the presence of an additional field-bath interaction. The problem is formulated within the framework of the generalized quantum Langevin equation, where the external confining potential modifies the random force correlations and the memory kernel of the environment, and the effective spring constant. Using the corresponding non-Markovian master equation, we examine the influence of the field-bath coupling on the temporal decay of the reduced density matrix of the system. We show that the additional interaction leads to an enhancement of the decoherence rate by altering the dissipative response of the bath. Thus our results shed light on the role of field-bath coupling in the quantum to classical transition of a CMO. The resulting fluctuation-dissipation relation is analyzed, and the position autocorrelation, position-velocity correlation and velocity autocorrelation are obtained explicitly. The dependence of these experimentally accessible quantities on the field-bath coupling parameter is discussed. We outline an experimental proposal for testing our theoretical predictions. The study sheds light on reservoir engineering which is central to quantum technologies.

papers.title: Inherent interpretability provides inherent value in quantum machine learning
papers.summary: The field of quantum machine learning (QML) evolved to value models believed to most directly rival those providing utility in classical ML, namely large-scale neural networks. This pursuit of quantum neural-network analogues has produced important theoretical insights for expressivity and trainability at scale; however, due to our inability to conduct large-scale empirical studies, this direction has contributed to skepticism that QML will provide a compelling application for quantum computers. In the meantime, classical ML has been learning a hard lesson with respect to deploying un-interpretable neural networks in the wild: model interpretability matters for human adoption. We adopt this broader ML perspective to encourage a research direction in QML that prioritizes discovering and understanding tools from quantum information theory that applied ML researchers can use to construct inherently interpretable models: models with intentional mathematical structure that guarantees domain-aligned behavior. We first exemplify this research direction through a thread of work in a neighboring area---Bayesian ML. Specifically, we discuss an efficient mathematical tool that emerged from a connection between Gaussian processes and Bayesian linear models, which has since been widely studied and used by applied researchers for problem-specific model design. We then discuss how prior QML research can be reframed as progress towards this direction, despite having been pursued with different goals in mind. Finally, we propose an initial sketch of future work in this direction, with the broader aim of better supporting the needs of applied ML researchers.

papers.title: New bound on $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell locality of a nonseparable Werner state
papers.summary: In many quantum applications it is important to know whether or not a Bell nonlocal two-qudit state exhibits its nonlocality under correlation scenarios with some given numbers $S_{1},S_{2}\geq1$ of generalized quantum measurements at two sites. In the present article, we find analytically a new general condition sufficient for a nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d\leq\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ to satisfy all Bell inequalities under every $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting correlation scenario with outcomes of an arbitrary spectral type, discrete or continuous $-$ that is, to be $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell local, for short. For a variety of measurement settings $S_{1}, S_{2}$, this new general bound is beyond (i) Werner's and Barrett's locality bounds for a nonseparable Werner state and (ii) the related result by Johnson and Viola [Phys. Rev. A 88, 032323 (2013)] on "sharability" of this state. When specialized to $d = 2$ and $\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\} = 2, 3$, our new general bound improves upon the corresponding results by Terhal et. al. in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 90, 157903 (2003)], moreover, for $d=\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\} = 2$, it reduces exactly to the bound derived for this case via the CHSH inequality. We prove also explicitly in operator terms the result of Terhal et. el. that every nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d >\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ is $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell local. The new results presented in this article are important for both the theory of Bell nonlocality and quantum applications based on this fundamental concept.

papers.title: Limitations on Joint Coherence Transfer in Quantum Thermodynamics
papers.summary: Coherences between different energy levels are strongly constrained by thermodynamics. Here we ask whether several coherence transfers that can be optimized separately can also be optimized simultaneously by the same thermodynamic process. Using an energy-resolved Stinespring representation of thermal operations, we express elementary transfer amplitudes as inner products of bath-weighted vectors. Joint saturation imposes collinearity and phase-closure conditions on these vectors, which must all arise from one energy-preserving system--bath unitary. This gives necessary compatibility conditions for arbitrary finite-dimensional Hamiltonians. We show that joint incompatibility persists in a system with both degenerate and nondegenerate energy levels: rigorous computer-assisted semidefinite-program bounds, combined with explicit thermal constructions, prove that three individual thermal optima cannot be approached simultaneously. We then determine how well different coherences can be protected when their optima are incompatible. For a four-level family at infinite temperature, we obtain the complete closed retention region and the cost of balancing the coherences relative to their individual optima. At positive temperature, covariance and Gibbs preservation permit joint retention that no thermal operation can approach. Finite-bath constructions and certified semidefinite relaxations bound the balanced thermal performance. When two coherences carry independent phases, these bounds describe simultaneous preservation of interference visibility and phase Fisher information.

papers.title: The Entanglement Content of Quantum Measurement Bases
papers.summary: Bell-state measurements are essential ingredients in many protocols for quantum information processing, ranging from quantum teleportation and dense coding to entanglement distribution in quantum networks. Their power relies on the fact that they are measurements in an entangled basis of a two-particle system and that the used Bell-state basis can be generated from a single Bell state by local unitary transformations. How can these measurements be generalized to more particles? We develop a general framework for this state-to-measurement problem: We introduce a hierarchy of classes of measurement bases, distinguished by the local transformations the parties may use for their generation from a single state. This leads to a generalization of the concept of maximally entangleable (or weighted hypergraph) states and the identification of a novel maximally entangled basis of four qubits, being a candidate for data-hiding tasks or distillation protocols. Finally, we prove that not all forms of entanglement can be encoded in an entire measurement basis.

papers.title: Measurements on the separated subsystems of an entangled state
papers.summary: The entangled states of composite quantum systems are well studied. The particle-like nature of these systems also means that, while entangled, they can be physically separated and measurements performed on the separated subsystems. Measurements on the separated subsystems A and B should pertain to vectors in the local Hilbert space of each subsystem, but to date it has not been clear how to elucidate the relevant states of the separated subsystems because it is not obvious how to resolve them from states given in the tensor product basis, except for the separable states. Here it is shown that the projections of any general entangled state that are detected by measurements on the separated subsystems can be obtained considering the corresponding (cosets of) states in the free vector space from which the tensor product space is defined. The result eliminates the need to invoke random collapse, and from this perspective nonlocality arises because of the way measurements on each separated subsystem projects possible measurement outcomes.

papers.title: Minimum Cardinalities of Multipartite Unextendible Product Bases
papers.summary: In quantum information theory, the state space of a multipartite quantum system is modeled by a tensor product. In the tensor-product space $\C^{d_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\C^{d_p}$, a nonzero vector is a \emph{product state} if it can be written as $\ket{\varphi_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\ket{\varphi_p}$ with $\ket{\varphi_j}\in\C^{d_j}\setminus\{0\}$. An \emph{unextendible product basis} (UPB) is a finite family of pairwise orthogonal product states such that no nonzero product state is orthogonal to all of them. UPBs play a key role in investigating quantum entanglement and nonlocal phenomena. Finding a smallest UPB is a natural extremal problem: it asks how few pairwise orthogonal product states suffice to prevent any further product state from being added. The general minimum-size problem for UPBs has been studied for over two decades since the seminal work of Alon and Lov\'asz. Let $f_m(d_1,\ldots,d_p)$ be the minimum cardinality of a UPB in the space, and let \(f_{LB}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)=1+\sum_{j=1}^{p}(d_j-1)\) be the natural lower bound. Alon and Lov\'asz determined exactly when \(f_m\) attains the lower bound \(f_{LB}\), but the obstructed multipartite cases remained open in general. We prove a stabilization theorem: for every non-all-qubit system with $p\ge3$, whenever the natural lower bound $f_{LB}$ is unattainable, the true minimum is exactly $f_{LB}+1$. Precisely, if the number of even local dimensions $d_i$ is positive and even, and at least one local dimension is greater than two, then \(f_m(d_1,\ldots,d_p)=f_{LB}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)+1\). The proof is built on a unified graph-theoretic framework. Our result, together with earlier work, settles the minimum size problem for UPBs in all finite quantum systems.

papers.title: Subsystem self-correction of the GKP qubit
papers.summary: Passive quantum error correction, also known as self-correction, is a holy grail in quantum information science. Recent theoretical advances suggest that the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code can exhibit self-correction properties, positioning it as a candidate for the realization of self-correcting quantum memories. In this article, we provide a self-contained derivation of the self-correcting behavior of the ideal GKP Hamiltonian, manifested in the Arrhenius type scaling of the logical lifetime, from a quantum-information perspective based on the subsystem code decomposition. When coupling through the physical quadrature $q$ and $p$, the detailed-balance jump operators decompose into a dominant part acting only on the gauge subsystem and a boundary term that acts non-trivially on the logical qubit. The boundary term is then exponentially suppressed by the Gibbs weights near the edge of the modular cells. In contrast to spin-based quantum memories such as the two-dimensional surface code, the GKP Hamiltonian realizes an effective string tension in modular phase space, whereby the energy cost increases as an error approaches the boundary of a logical sector.

papers.title: Exact computation of quantum wave functions for nonlinear potentials
papers.summary: Recent work shows that the Schr\"odinger equation can be solved exactly based only on classical least action. The computation is based on first computing the multi-valued action solutions of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, computing the classical propagated density along all stationary action multipaths, and finally constructing the exact kernel and wave function based on these classical multi-valued quantities alone. The method requires that the propagated classical square root density along each stationary action path is harmonic, as is the case for basic examples such as e.g., the double-slit, quantum tunneling, or the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen experiment. For more complex cases, residual Bohm-like quantum potentials along each stationary action path can be eliminated through a time-rescaling. This paper proposes an extended version of the above construction which avoids the need for time-rescaling even in the most general cases. This is achieved by introducing in the Hamilton-Jacobi equation a real viscosity term, which classically simply corresponds to replacing a lumped parameter model with a continuum model including a volumetric stress tensor. This keeps the earlier construction unchanged, except that the real stationary action multipaths are now real stationary viscous action multipaths defined with respect to an associated modified Lagrangian. As in the earlier version, the construction extends straightforwardly to the special and general relativistic contexts, thus describing in a common language the quantum, classical, and relativistic cases. Note that the global Bohm potential term in the lumped Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with a Madelung transform does not have a classical equivalent, while the volumetric stress tensor term in our viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation directly represents the real paths of a classical deformed particle field.

papers.title: Unconditional Security of Discrete-Modulated CV-QKD from Infinite-Dimensional MEAT
papers.summary: Discrete-Modulated (DM) Continuous-Variable (CV) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an experimentally attractive approach to quantum cryptography, offering high key rates over metropolitan-scale distances while relying on state-of-the-art telecom infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap has remained between this experimental promise and rigorous security: for more than two decades, DM CV-QKD has lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Existing works either restrict the adversary to collective attacks, impose additional finite-dimensional assumptions, apply only to specific modulation formats, or fail to recover the known asymptotic rates. Here, we resolve this longstanding problem by establishing the first complete composable finite-size security proof for DM CV-QKD protocols against coherent attacks, incorporating imperfect detectors and both fixed- and variable-length protocol variants. Our proof introduces two central results of broader interest: an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and a rigorous dimension-reduction technique that makes the infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable. The resulting key rates recover the known asymptotic rates and outperform established finite-size bounds based on collective attacks, while yielding positive key rates beyond $70$km for experimentally relevant block sizes and parameters. Thus, our work closes a longstanding gap and places an experimentally attractive class of CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing and provides a pathway towards their practical deployment.

papers.title: Approximate synthesis of general single-qubit unitaries over the Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ gate set
papers.summary: For the standard Clifford+$T$ gate set, deterministic, ancilla-free synthesis now attains the minimal $T$-count for general single-qubit unitaries (Morisaki et al., arXiv:2510.05816). The $\sqrt{T}$ gate rotates by half the angle of $T$, generating a finer lattice of implementable operations. Access to this magic state is expected to lower the cost of deterministic and ancilla-free synthesis of general single-qubit unitaries (Kliuchnikov et al., arXiv:2203.10064), but no direct Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ algorithm existed for this case. We provide one by extending the integer lattice-point enumeration method of Morisaki et al. We adopt a resource state cost model based on the magic-state catalysis approach of Gidney and Fowler (arXiv:1812.01238). On Haar-random targets synthesized to precisions ranging from $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ to $10^{-8}$, the cost of Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ circuits scales as $2.4\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$ compared to $3.0\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$ for $T$-count-optimal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Once a one-time catalyst state is amortized, the Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ circuits are never costlier than their Clifford+$T$ counterparts.

papers.title: Eigenvalue-by-Eigenvalue Comparison of a Sierra--Rodr\'iguez-Laguna-Type Spectrum with the Riemann Zeros
papers.summary: We study the self-adjoint extension of the Sierra--Rodr\'iguez-Laguna (SR) $H=xp$-type Hamiltonian $\widehat H_{SR}$. Its discrete spectrum is fixed by the equation $\mathrm{Re}\!\left[e^{-i\theta/2}K_{1/2+iE/2}(2\pi)\right]=0$. We solve this equation numerically for $\theta=1.417\pi$ and obtain the first 606 eigenvalues $E_n$. We compare them, one by one, with the ordinates $\gamma_n$ of the first 606 nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Using the steepest-descent (saddle-point) method for the modified Bessel function, together with the Riemann--von Mangoldt formula, we derive a closed-form prediction for $E_n-\gamma_n$ in terms of the Lambert-$W$ function: $E_n-\gamma_n\simeq(\theta-\pi/4)/[1+W(n/e)]$, which decays only like $1/\ln n$. Here the $n$-th numerical root corresponds to the $(n-2)$-th root of the asymptotic quantization condition. The leading-order phase of $K_{1/2+iE/2}(2\pi)$ agrees with a known rigorous asymptotic formula for modified Bessel functions of large imaginary order. The prediction is checked against the first $10^5$ tabulated zeta zeros (A.~Odlyzko): the measured coefficient of $1/[1+W(n/e)]$ is $3.666$ (mean) and $3.667$ (median) for $n\ge10^3$, in agreement with $\theta-\pi/4=3.666$. The scatter of $E_n-\gamma_n$ around this smooth curve comes from the fluctuating term $S(T)$ of the zero-counting function, which the spectrum $E_n$ does not contain.

papers.title: The coupler Eve did not monitor: non-signalling reports from interacting cavities
papers.summary: Eve receives genuine average photon counts from two opaque devices, finds input-independent single-party report distributions, and sees little activity in a specified leakage monitor. Do these observations establish physical isolation? We construct a cavity-based counterexample. Independently operated controls activate a shared interaction after the inputs arrive. Internal block measurements yield a CHSH score $S=13/4$ for four repetitions, approaching $4$ for large blocks. A fresh shared random bit symmetrizes the binary results without changing their parity; local preparation of vacuum or one-photon output states then produces truthful photon-number reports with exactly non-signalling marginals. A dispersive-bus model also permits weak monitored leakage; an illustrative dissipative calculation gives $S\simeq3.1702$ with ideal output encoding. These scores exceed $2\sqrt2$ because the devices interact during their response, not because quantum mechanics is violated. The construction separates honest measurement, non-signalling reported statistics, and causal isolation, while making the additional randomness, preparation, and monitoring assumptions explicit.

papers.title: Breakdown of thermalization in quantum spin systems with long-range interactions
papers.summary: Quantum thermalization of closed systems -- i.e. the relaxation of local properties to their thermodynamic value along the Hamiltonian evolution -- is generically expected in non-integrable systems at finite energy density. In this work we show that quantum spin systems with at least one spin component coupled through long-range ferromagnetic interactions, and a second spin component coupled to a field, cannot in general thermalize to a paramagnetic state whenever they have a finite, negative energy per spin. The long-range interactions we consider decay as a power law of the distance, $\sim r^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha < d$, where $d$ is the number of spatial dimensions of the system. The lack of thermalization is generic to an infinite family of Hamiltonians, and it is not associated to any form of integrability. It can instead be understood by the anomalous features of the thermodynamics of the system in the paramagnetic phase, which cannot be reflected in the properties of the eigenstates. This leads to a breakdown of eigenstate typicality and of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Interestingly, the non-thermal states emerging at long times in the dynamics display long-range multipartite entanglement, elevating the breakdown of thermalization to a resource.

u}$, where each $

u$ contains the pure states compatible with $
u$. We define the quantum Boltzmann entropy for a macro state $

u) = k_{\mathrm{B}} \log \dim \mathscr{H}_{
u}$, where $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant. Goldstein et al. [http://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11870] have suggested, as a version of the second law of thermodynamics, that $S_\mathrm{qB}$ predominantly increases with time for realistic macroscopic systems. papers.title: Scalable Tomography of Coherent Noise via Stabilizer-Code Polarization
papers.summary: Coherent errors accumulate linearly rather than diffusively, making them invisible to Pauli-twirl-based characterization. This poses a central challenge for quantum error correction, yet its characterization typically requires multi-qubit process tomography whose cost grows exponentially with system size. We show that measurement-free error correction projects arbitrary few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed single-logical-qubit effective channel, enabling tomography at constant cost. Exploiting the polarization effects of bit-flip and phase-flip codes, we construct a concatenated effective-channel fingerprint and prove, by a parity-based contradiction argument, that the observation map is globally injective over a prescribed coherent-noise family; hence the underlying noise parameters are uniquely recovered without any sparsity or low-rank assumptions. We further corroborate the theoretical guarantee by a synthetic numerical test: over 500 randomly sampled points in the compact parameter domain, the $64\times11$ Jacobian of the concatenated fingerprint maintains full column rank with a strictly positive smallest singular value in every case, confirming that all 11 parameter directions remain first-order identifiable throughout the region. The recovered coherent noise model can be fed into decoding algorithms; relative to independent noise priors, we expect this to reduce the logical error rate for surface-code decoders. The protocol offers a scalable route to coherent-noise identification whenever the noise admits a moderate-dimensional parameterization.

papers.title: Anticommuting Displacement Operators, Exact Pauli Algebras,and the Singlet State from the Oscillator Vacuum
papers.summary: We give an explicit construction of a pair of anticommuting Weyl displacement operators for a harmonic oscillator and use bounded functional calculus to obtain exact dichotomic representatives of the Pauli algebra. Two independent oscillators provide commuting Pauli algebras for Alice and Bob. The standard singlet-sector projector, written entirely in terms of these bounded oscillator observables, is then applied to the two-oscillator vacuum. We show explicitly that the projected vacuum has nonzero norm, so its normalization is well defined, has the exact singlet correlations, and reaches the Tsirelson value $2\sqrt2$ for the usual Bell--CHSH settings. We also clarify that the construction generally realizes a singlet sector with multiplicity, rather than selecting a unique vector in the full oscillator Hilbert space, and we compare the construction with the older pseudospin approach to continuous-variable Bell tests.

papers.title: PPT-assisted capacities of bosonic Gaussian channels
papers.summary: We determine the exact quantum communication and entanglement-distribution capacities of three fundamental bosonic channels, namely thermal loss, thermal amplification and additive Gaussian noise, assisted by operations that completely preserve positive partial transpose (PPT). These operations are more powerful than local operations and classical communication (LOCC), but cannot generate distillable entanglement on their own. For thermal loss, the unconstrained capacity coincides with the Pirandola-Laurenza-Ottaviani-Banchi (PLOB) bound throughout the non-entanglement-breaking regime. The corresponding upper bounds are also attained for thermal amplification and additive noise. We extend these results to energy-constrained communication, establishing exact capacities for all three channels at every prescribed mean input energy. Our results solve a class of bosonic capacity problems under PPT assistance and establish exact benchmarks for determining whether the same communication rates can be achieved via LOCC alone.
